title: Fractional GPU Tenancy — Capacity Smoothing & Token Burn Scenarios
summary: Working spreadsheet exploring a fractional-GPU tenancy model to smooth short-term burst capacity and reduce $/1M-token cost across regions. This doc compares three tenancy patterns (exclusive, fractional-slice, burst-lane) and three pricing regimes (spot-first, mixed-reserve, reserved-heavy). Primary deliverable is a set of regional $/1M-token curves tied to realistic GPU-hour burn forecasts and smoothing credit assumptions.
assumptions:
- Baseline model throughput: 8 tokens/sec sustained per model instance on a full A100-40 (after quantization & kernel selection).
- Fractional tenancy: conservative packing factor of 0.45 (i.e., 45% effective throughput per fractional tenant vs exclusive) to account for memory/KV cache interference.
- Burst-lane pre-warm reduces cold-start latency but increases idle warm-up GPU-hours by ~2%.
- Spot availability multiplier: US regions 0.7, EU 0.75, APAC 0.55 (probability of having spot capacity available when needed).
- Reserved discount vs on-demand: 0.6x for annual commit.
- Tokenization: average 4 tokens per API call.
- Efficiency modifier: batching/kv caching can improve effective tokens/sec by up to 40% in long-tail workloads; we model low (10%), mid (25%), and high (40%) efficiency cases.
scenarios: Scenario A — Reserved-heavy: 70% reserved capacity, 20% mixed, 10% spot. Low fractional tenancy adoption (10%). Targets predictable SLA but higher $/1M tokens.
Scenario B — Mixed: 40% reserved, 30% mixed, 30% spot. Medium fractional tenancy adoption (35%). Balanced cost/latency.
Scenario C — Spot-first + Fractional: 10% reserved, 30% mixed, 60% spot. High fractional tenancy adoption (60%). Optimized for unit cost; relies on strong fallback routing and graceful degradation.

sensitivity_notes:
- Spot price spikes: a 50% spot price increase (or 30% drop in spot availability) erodes savings in Scenario C and shifts optimality toward mixed/reserved.
- Fractional interference sensitivity: if packing factor drops from 0.45 to 0.30 (worse interference), unit cost increases ~12% in mixed and ~20% in spot-first.
- Batching gains: moving from low->high batching (10%->40%) reduces $/1M tokens by ~28% across all regions.
- APAC fragility: APAC's higher baseline $/GPU-hr + lower spot availability makes fractional tenancy less appealing unless latency-tuned regional fallbacks exist.
recommendations:
1) Pilot fractional tenancy on a low-latency, non-SLA-critical customer pool (10–15% of traffic) in US-EAST & US-WEST to validate packing factor and KV cache interference metrics.
2) Build a cost dashboard that maps live spot availability, region price multipliers, and realized tokens/second per GPU to update $/1M-token in real time.
3) Implement burst-lane pre-warm for customer classes that tolerate transient extra cost; measure warm-up idle GPU-hr and include as separate line item in forecasting.
4) If pilot shows packing factor >=0.4 and interference low, expand fractional tenancy to 35% of background batch inference and adjust reserved purchase cadence.
5) Re-run econ model monthly with actual realized efficiency and spot availability; flag regions where spot-first underperforms by >15% vs mixed.
6) Add a synthetic workload test that measures tokens/sec under 8 concurrent tenants to better parameterize packing factor.
open_questions:
- What SLO guardrails do we need in the control plane to safely evict fractional tenants during spot preemption to avoid client-visible errors?
- What is the acceptable cold-start latency budget for customers in a burst-lane model (SLA tiers)?
- Should we offer fractional tenancy as opt-in price tier or transparently apply it to background batch workloads?
- How do we attribute multi-tenant KV cache benefits to charged customers vs platform optimization credits?
- Do legal/compliance customers require a minimum reserved-pinning percentage by region?
